title: Night Photography: Settings for City Lights, Trails and Stars — cv.cm
description: Night photography settings for cameras and phones: handheld vs tripod, night mode, blue hour, light trails, stars with the 500 and NPF rules, and focus in the dark.
h1: What are the best settings for night photography?
answer: On a tripod, start at f/8, ISO 100 and adjust the shutter from 1 to 30 seconds for city scenes and light trails. Handheld, use the widest aperture, a shutter near 1/focal length with stabilization, and ISO 1600 to 6400. For stars, use f/2.8 or wider, ISO 3200 to 6400 and 8 to 20 seconds. On a phone, let night mode run and hold still or rest the phone.

sections.h: Two ways to shoot at night
body: A lit street at night has roughly 10 stops less light than a sunny day, and a starry sky far more than that. The camera can only make up for it in three ways: open the aperture, raise ISO, or keep the shutter open longer. Which one you choose depends on one question: is the camera held in your hands, or resting on something solid?

ul: Handheld: the shutter must stay short enough to avoid shake, so you use a wide aperture and high ISO. You get more noise and less depth of field, but you can move freely and photograph people.

Tripod or a solid surface: the shutter can stay open for seconds, so ISO can stay low and the aperture can be small. Detail is much higher and moving lights turn into smooth trails. Moving people turn into blurs or disappear.

body: Phones combine both ideas. Night mode takes many short frames and merges them, and when the phone detects a tripod it allows a longer total capture.

body: Use manual mode on a tripod so the exposure does not change between frames. Check the histogram after each test shot: a night scene should have most of the graph on the left, but the bright windows and signs should not be pressed against the right edge. If they are, shorten the shutter.

White balance changes the mood a lot. Daylight (about 5,200 K) keeps sodium street lights warm orange. Tungsten (about 3,200 K) makes them whiter and the sky bluer. For stars, about 3,500 to 4,000 K gives a natural dark blue sky. Shoot RAW if you can, so you can decide later.

The reciprocal rule says the slowest safe handheld shutter is about 1 divided by the full-frame-equivalent focal length: 1/50 s for a 50 mm lens on full frame, or about 1/80 s for a 50 mm lens on an APS-C camera with a 1.5x crop. Image stabilization in the lens or body typically lets you go 2 to 4 stops slower, so 1/50 s can become 1/15 or even 1/8 s for still scenes. Stabilization does not stop people from moving, so keep at least 1/60 to 1/125 s for faces.

ul: Set auto ISO with a minimum shutter speed, and allow ISO up to 6400 or 12800. A sharp noisy photo is better than a blurry clean one.
Exhale, press the shutter gently, and take three frames in a row; one is usually sharper.
Lean against a lamp post, rest the camera on a railing, or press it against a wall.
Use a fast prime lens (f/1.4 to f/2) if you have one; it gathers 1 to 3 stops (2 to 8 times) more light than an f/2.8 to f/4 zoom.
Do not underexpose to protect the shutter speed and then brighten later. That shows more noise than using the higher ISO in the first place.

sections.h: Blue hour, city lights and light trails
body: The best time for cityscapes is often not full darkness but blue hour, the period after sunset when the sky is deep blue and the city lights are on. Sky and buildings are then close in brightness, so one exposure records both. It lasts roughly 20 to 40 minutes, depending on your latitude and the season. Arrive before sunset to set up the tripod and composition while you can still see. See the golden hour guide for how to look up the times.

For light trails, find a high place overlooking a busy road, a bridge, or a bend where cars come toward you and drive away, so you get both white headlights and red tail lights. Set the camera on a tripod, f/8 to f/11, ISO 100, and start with 15 seconds. At 1 to 2 seconds the trails are short and broken; at 15 to 30 seconds they become long continuous lines. Traffic lights stop the flow, so time your exposure to the green phase.
A small aperture such as f/11 to f/16 makes street lights and bright windows appear as small stars with points. The number of points depends on the aperture blades in the lens.

Stars need a dark place, far from city lights, on a clear night near a new moon. Use a wide lens (14 to 24 mm on full frame) at its widest aperture, ideally f/2.8 or faster, and start with ISO 3200 to 6400 and about 15 seconds.
The Earth turns, so stars move across the frame. If the shutter is too long, they become short lines. Two rules estimate the limit:

ul: 500 rule: maximum seconds is about 500 divided by the full-frame-equivalent focal length. A 20 mm lens on full frame gives 25 s. The same lens on an APS-C camera (1.5x crop) gives 500 / 30, about 16 s. On modern high-resolution sensors, trailing is visible earlier, so many photographers use 300 or 400 instead of 500.

NPF rule: a more accurate estimate that also includes the aperture and the sensor's pixel size. Astronomy and photo-planning apps calculate it for your camera and lens. It usually gives a shorter time than the 500 rule.

body: For star trails, do the opposite: take many 20 to 30 second exposures in a row for 30 minutes or more with the camera's interval timer, then combine them with stacking software. A single very long exposure also works but gets noisy and warm on many sensors.

Focus is the hardest part. Autofocus usually fails in the dark, and the infinity mark on many lenses is not exact. Switch to manual focus, magnify the live view as much as you can on the brightest star or a distant light, and turn the ring slowly until the point is smallest. Then do not touch the ring; a piece of tape helps. Check focus again on the first photo at full magnification.

ol: Use the 1x main camera. It has the largest sensor and widest aperture; the telephoto and ultra-wide cameras are much noisier at night, and many phones crop the 1x camera instead anyway.
Let night mode turn on by itself. On iPhone the night mode icon turns yellow; on Pixel it is Night Sight.
Tap the brightest important area and lower exposure slightly so signs and lamps keep their color.
Hold still until the capture ends. If iPhone shows crosshairs, line them up. Better, rest the phone on a wall or a small tripod and use a 3 second timer.

On a tripod, many phones allow a longer capture time. Pixel phones switch to an astrophotography mode for stars when the phone is on a stand; Google suggests shooting at least 45 to 90 minutes after sunset, away from city lights.
For light trails, some phones have a long-exposure or motion mode, and some have a Pro mode where you can set a shutter of several seconds on a tripod.
Turn off the flash for scenes. It only lights a few metres and makes the background black.

body: Phone night photos sometimes look brighter than the scene really was. If you want it to feel like night, lower the exposure before you shoot or in editing.

body: Long exposure noise reduction, if your camera has it, takes a dark frame after each long exposure and subtracts hot pixels. It doubles the wait, so turn it off when you shoot star trails as a sequence.

body.note: Go to dark places with a friend, tell someone your plan, and carry a torch with a red mode to protect your night vision. Do not stand on roads or rail lines for light trails. Tripods are not allowed on some bridges, viewpoints and buildings, and some parks close at night or need a permit; check the rules first.

faq.q: What is the 500 rule in night photography?
faq.a: It estimates the longest shutter time before stars start to trail: 500 divided by the full-frame-equivalent focal length. A 24 mm lens gives about 20 s. On high-resolution cameras use 300 or 400, or the NPF rule, for sharper stars.

faq.q: Can you do night photography without a tripod?
faq.a: Yes, for streets, people and lit buildings. Use a fast lens, stabilization, a shutter near 1/focal length and high ISO, and brace the camera on something solid. Light trails, stars and low-noise cityscapes need a tripod or a stable surface.

faq.q: Why are my night photos blurry?
faq.a: Either the camera moved during a long shutter, the subject moved, or focus missed in the dark. Use a faster shutter or a tripod with a timer, and focus manually on a bright point with the view magnified.

faq.q: What ISO should I use at night?
faq.a: ISO 100 on a tripod for city scenes and trails. ISO 1600 to 6400 handheld and 3200 to 6400 for stars. Modern cameras handle these values well; correct exposure matters more than low ISO.

faq.q: How do I photograph the moon at night?
faq.a: The moon is lit by direct sunlight, so it needs daylight-like settings, not night settings: about f/11 and a shutter of 1/ISO. See the moon guide for lenses, phone tips and timing.
